prompt: Who designed C++?
explanation: Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ at Bell Labs starting in 1979 as 'C with Classes'.

prompt: What does RAII stand for in C++?
explanation: RAII ties resource lifetimes to object lifetimes. Constructors acquire; destructors release. The defining C++ idiom.

prompt: In C++, the destructor runs automatically when an object goes out of scope.
explanation: This deterministic cleanup is what enables RAII and exception safety. Different from Java's non-deterministic finalization.

prompt: What does the 'Rule of Zero' suggest?
options: Prefer types whose members handle resources, so you write none of the special members
correctAnswer: Prefer types whose members handle resources, so you write none of the special members
explanation: With std::vector, std::unique_ptr, std::string handling their own resources, your class can use the synthesized defaults — no manual memory code.

prompt: What standard library type holds a mutex lock for the duration of a scope, releasing on destruction?
explanation: std::lock_guard (and std::scoped_lock for multiple locks) demonstrates RAII for synchronization. Lock acquired in constructor; released in destructor.

prompt: Match each C++ class member to its role:

pairs.right: Cleans up when the object dies
Creates a new object as a copy of an existing one

explanation: These four (plus assignment versions) are the special member functions. The Rule of Five says: write all of them or none.

prompt: RAII makes exception-safe code natural because destructors run during stack unwinding.
explanation: When an exception propagates, all in-scope objects' destructors run, releasing resources. This is why C++ can use exceptions safely without try-with-resources.

Otherwise the default copy will alias data and double-free in destructors. Or use std::vector<char> and follow the Rule of Zero.

prompt: In C++, when are templates instantiated?
options: At compile time, once per type used
correctAnswer: At compile time, once per type used
explanation: Each unique template instantiation produces compiled code. This gives zero-overhead generics at the cost of larger binaries.

prompt: What C++20 feature lets you constrain template parameters with named requirements?
explanation: Concepts (template <std::integral T>) provide named, composable type constraints. They dramatically improve template error messages.

prompt: std::vector<bool> is a special-cased template instantiation that packs bits.
explanation: std::vector<bool> is a partial specialization storing 1 bit per element. Famously controversial because it doesn't behave like other vectors.

prompt: What does SFINAE mean in C++?
options: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error
Strict Function Implementation Needs A Header
Static Field Initialization Not An Element
correctAnswer: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error
explanation: If a template substitution fails, the compiler removes that overload from consideration rather than erroring. The basis for many template tricks (now mostly replaced by concepts).

prompt: What keyword marks a function as evaluable at compile time?
explanation: constexpr functions can run at compile time when given constant arguments. Each new C++ standard expands what's allowed inside constexpr.

prompt: Match each template tool to its purpose:

pairs.right: Override behavior for a specific type

explanation: These are the building blocks of generic programming in modern C++.

prompt: How does C++ generic code differ from Java generics?
options: C++ generates new code per type at compile time; Java erases types and uses Object internally
correctAnswer: C++ generates new code per type at compile time; Java erases types and uses Object internally
explanation: C++ templates: monomorphization, zero overhead, longer compiles. Java generics: type erasure at runtime, smaller binaries, some runtime cost.

prompt: Find the error in this template:
steps: T max(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }
// 'no matching function for call to max(int, double)'
explanation: Step 3 is the call-site mistake. The template requires both args be the SAME T. max(3, 5.0) gives int and double, no single T satisfies. Fix: explicitly cast (max(3.0, 5.0)), use two type params (template<typename A, typename B>), or name the type explicitly: max<double>(3, 5.0). (std::max has exactly the same restriction, so std::max(3, 5.0) fails too.)

prompt: What does std::move do?
options: Copies the value to a new location
Casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference, signaling that resources may be stolen
correctAnswer: Casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference, signaling that resources may be stolen
explanation: std::move doesn't move anything itself; it just casts. The actual move happens in the assignment/constructor that receives the rvalue reference.

prompt: What smart pointer represents single, exclusive ownership of a heap object?
explanation: std::unique_ptr is move-only. Replaces 99% of raw owning pointers in modern C++. Zero overhead vs raw pointer.

prompt: std::shared_ptr uses reference counting to manage shared ownership.
explanation: Each shared_ptr increments an atomic counter. When the count drops to zero, the object is deleted. Has overhead vs unique_ptr.

prompt: Why might you use std::weak_ptr alongside std::shared_ptr?
options: To break reference cycles that would otherwise leak memory
weak_ptr is required by the standard
correctAnswer: To break reference cycles that would otherwise leak memory
explanation: In a parent/child graph, parent owns children with shared_ptr but children observe parent with weak_ptr. Without this, the cycle keeps each side alive indefinitely.

prompt: What helper function preferred over `new` constructs a unique_ptr atomically and exception-safely?
explanation: std::make_unique<T>(args...) creates a T on the heap and wraps it in a unique_ptr in one step. Safer than new because it can't leak between allocation and ownership.

prompt: In modern C++, raw `new` and `delete` should be rare in application code.
explanation: std::make_unique, std::vector, std::string handle dynamic allocation safely. Raw new/delete is reserved for low-level libraries and legacy code.

prompt: Which is the default-recommended STL container for most uses?
explanation: std::vector wins on cache locality, simplicity, and performance for the vast majority of use cases. Reach for others only when you have a reason.

prompt: What STL container is a hash table providing O(1) average-time operations?
explanation: std::unordered_map (added in C++11) is the standard hash map. std::map is sorted (typically a red-black tree).

prompt: STL algorithms work on any container that exposes the appropriate iterators.
explanation: std::sort, std::find, std::accumulate operate via iterators. The same algorithm works on vector, deque, array, raw pointer ranges, etc.

prompt: What does a C++ lambda capture clause '[&]' mean?
options: Capture all referenced outer variables by reference
correctAnswer: Capture all referenced outer variables by reference
explanation: [&] captures everything by reference. [=] captures by value. [x] captures only x by value; [&x] only x by reference. Mix as needed.

prompt: What C++20 library provides lazy, composable view pipelines on collections?
explanation: std::ranges enables 'vec | filter(...) | transform(...)' style pipelines. Often as fast as hand-written loops, much more readable.

prompt: Match each STL algorithm to its purpose:
explanation: These four cover much of common data-transformation work. The library has dozens more.

prompt: Which feature was introduced in C++11?
explanation: Lambdas debuted in C++11 along with auto, range-for, smart pointers, move semantics, and the threading library. Modules and concepts came in C++20; coroutines also C++20.

prompt: What C++17 type represents 'either a value or absence of one' (similar to Maybe/Option)?
explanation: std::optional<T> wraps a value-or-empty. Cleaner than NULL pointers or special sentinel values. C++23 added monadic operations like and_then, transform.

prompt: C++20 introduced four major features: Concepts, Ranges, Modules, and Coroutines.
explanation: These are the headline C++20 additions. Together they reshape how modern C++ code is written.

prompt: What C++23 type provides Rust-style error handling, holding either a value or an error?
explanation: std::expected<T, E> mirrors Rust's Result. Cleaner than exceptions for recoverable errors and more discoverable than error codes.

prompt: Find the error in this argument:
steps: I follow the Rule of Zero
Therefore my code is memory-safe like Rust
explanation: Step 5 is overconfident. Modern C++ idioms eliminate MANY memory bugs but not all: dangling references, iterator invalidation, data races, lifetime errors with shared_ptr cycles. Rust's borrow checker provides compile-time guarantees C++ doesn't have. Modern C++ is much safer than C++03 but still requires discipline.
